stage_state.summary_md:
## Coordinating Retirement
BA wanted a celebratory retirement at the end of the summer schedule (October), coordinating with Air France. Air France initially agreed but then decided to retire in May, just weeks away, reflecting the at-odds attitudes and the impossibility of a celebratory dual retirement in France post-accident.

## Announcing the Decision
An extraordinary Forum 150 meeting (top 150 managers) was set for 9 April 2003, but Bannister noted that was the 34th anniversary of British Concorde’s first flight, so it moved to 10 April. Bannister, in uniform, presented the rationale. The “Marmite factor” emerged: two-thirds sad, remainder relieved, no ambivalence—presaging public reaction. A press release followed an hour later.

## Public Face and Key Messages
Bannister became company spokesman. Key points: a commercial decision driven by factors beyond control; customers would be cared for on upgraded 747 Club/First. Despite earlier opposition, he accepted the role to ensure a dignified celebration, not a wake. At the press conference, when asked why, he hesitated then said: “It’s the right decision at the right time for the right reasons”—a mantra that became the party line, though he’d internally thought it wrong.

## Handling Tough Questions
- **Why spend to return to service only to retire?** Not due to the accident; sound commercial reasons.
- **Why not give it to Richard Branson?** Anticipated: Virgin would either make BA look incompetent or blame BA if it failed. Official response: “Because the aeroplane was originally funded by the UK government, the decision to transfer ownership isn’t ours to make.” A senior Virgin pilot later told Bannister it would “probably send us bust!”—the costs would have killed Virgin.
- **Keep one for air shows?** Concorde required a Certificate of Airworthiness and Type Certificate, far costlier than the Vulcan’s Permit to Fly. Infrastructure cost was £60 million p.a., set to rise by £40 million, unchanged whether one or seven aircraft. Even at £50 million, that’s £1 million a week. Airbus, the Type Certificate holder, was uninterested, focusing on A380 and A320, and the air-intake computer technology was proprietary and secret (used in military aircraft). No other realistic candidate; Airbus had no compulsion to transfer.

## Shifting Public Sentiment
By summer, discussion turned to legacy: UK’s achievement, doing what Americans hadn’t. People shared stories of relatives flying. The celebration honored all—designers, builders, crew, public. Edward de Bono said Concorde appealed to both brain hemispheres; Bannister felt simpler: Brits felt ownership—“That’s my Concorde up there.”
